posts.content:
The last three years have been pretty intense for me. I’ve found myself in the middle of a lot of changes, both personal and professional, and even today they still leave me with a strong sense of uncertainty about what the next few years will look like.

I’m raising twins, who are now three years old, and nobody really prepared me for what that would mean. Sure, I read books and took a few online courses, but then reality happens, and there are so many variables that things rarely go the way you expect. Becoming a parent also forces you to discover sides of yourself you didn’t even know were there, things that were probably sitting somewhere in the background, waiting for a child to bring them out. So I haven’t just had to take care of them. I’ve also had to start changing myself, mostly to avoid completely losing my mind in the process.

And while all of this was happening, AI exploded into our lives and started making us question what our jobs will even look like, especially in tech. For the past three years, I’ve basically spent every day trying to understand where all of this is going, studying everything I can around AI engineering and agentic systems. 

At the same time, the roles themselves are changing, and that’s actually one of the reasons I wanted to explore this topic with my podcast, The Product Engineers Podcast. It also pushed me to study things outside my usual comfort zone, like Product Discovery and UX/UI design, because I’d rather prepare now than wait until this new way of working is suddenly expected from all of us. And obviously, this is my bet on the future. You might see things completely differently.

Now add some economic instability on top of that. The market for developers hasn’t exactly been amazing lately, and companies have become VERY demanding. It sometimes feels like you need to be a superstar just to get into a team. And as much as I’d love to be a superstar, you can probably imagine how difficult that is when you’re trying to be a parent, learn a bunch of new things, and, you know, actually do your job at the same time.

It’s not easy to say, but I think people who don’t have kids or too many responsibilities on their shoulders right now simply have more room to take advantage of the opportunities that are coming. Okay, I’ll stop complaining like a old man :)

The rules of the game have changed, and I don’t think there’s much we can do about it other than grit our teeth, adapt, and do the best we can.

I believe that in the next few years, “I’m not a designer” will become a weak excuse.

AI can already generate a landing page, a dashboard, an onboarding flow, a pricing table, or a whole UI from a rough prompt. Most of the time, it will give you something that looks decent enough at first glance. But “looks decent” is not the same as “works well”.

Every time we decide whether a flow is clear, whether the copy reduces confusion, whether the user understands what happens next, whether a familiar pattern is better than a clever new one, that’s design. The same way AI coding doesn’t remove the need to understand software design, AI-generated interfaces won’t remove the need to understand product design.

My bet: the people who train that muscle, engineers included, will stand out a lot more than people expect. A good eye for design will become a multiplier when everything works and feels average.

posts.content:
I secretly hope that “software factories” become a reliable thing.

I imagine product engineers owning one product problem end to end: talking to users, understanding the pain, exploring solutions, defining scenarios, steering the factory, shipping, and learning from what happens.

Maybe 80% of their time goes into finding and executing on the problem, and 20% into overseeing the factory doing more of the implementation work.

The team around them would look different too.

PMs would work at the level of the broader product context. They would connect individual problems to strategy, monitoring bets, help deciding where attention should go, and keep the whole product moving in a coherent direction.

Product engineers would work one level closer to the user. Instead of receiving a solution disguised as a ticket, they would own a problem and the outcome attached to it.

And specialists (different types of designers, researchers, data scientists, security engineers, platform engineers) would join only when the job requires high expertise in their field.

One person owns the scene from beginning to end, while specialists step in when the work needs lighting, sound, effects, or a difficult shot. 
Someone still protects the direction of the whole film, but nobody spends their day throwing half-finished artefacts over a wall.

The software factory sits underneath this team. It can build, test, deploy, observe, and revise, but the team still frames the problem, defines the boundaries, and judges whether the outcome is actually good.

And honestly, that’s the future I want: fewer people coordinating the delivery of features, and more people taking responsibility for product problems from beginning to end.

Would you want to work in a team shaped like this?

postedAt.postedAgoText: 1 month ago • Visible to anyone on or off LinkedIn

posts.content:
Every time I see “coding is solved,” I’m not quite sure what people mean by “coding.” Anyone who's been around building software for a while knows that software engineering is not one thing! There's the design part, for example, what should we create, where the boundaries are, what trade-offs are acceptable, and what the consequences are when anything goes wrong.

And then there's a lot of what we call "plumbing", like choosing tools, configuring them, integrating them into the codebase, calling APIs, publishing messages, consuming events, handling retries and timeouts, following framework conventions, fixing misconfigurations. 

I think that distinction is quite important when we talk about AI coding. “Can AI code?” is not a very useful question. A better one is: which parts of software engineering can we safely hand over to AI, and which parts still need close human control?

For plumbing, integrations, and a lot of debugging, I’m increasingly happy to hand over the keyboard. These problems are usually well understood, there are established patterns, and someone has implemented roughly the same thing ten thousand times already. AI is very good at reading documentation, finding those patterns, applying them, and getting through a lot of the repetitive work faster than we can.

The parts I’m much less willing to delegate blindly are design, business logic, and testing. That’s where the important decisions live. What should the system actually do? What assumptions are we making? Which trade-off is acceptable? What behaviour must never break? How do we know the agent built the right thing rather than merely something that compiles?

So I think “coding is solved” is the wrong framing. A lot of repetitive implementation work is becoming automated, and that’s a good thing. It was necessary work, not less valuable work, but much of it was repetitive rather than creative.

If a robot wants to configure libraries, wire up another API, and spend its afternoon arguing with a YAML file, I’m perfectly happy to let it.

posts.content:
Change my mind: in AI coding, we're reinventing the wheel over and over. Take "context engineering", that's something we've been doing for ages, we just called it "software design".

Every time we designed a codebase to be maintainable, extensible, and testable, that's exactly what we were doing.

Clear separation of concerns. Domains. Working against interfaces. Business logic isolated from infrastructure: the same old ideas that made codebases easier for humans to reason about.

When a system is modularised correctly, an agent doesn't need to scan the entire codebase to find what it needs. Less wasted tokens, less irrelevant code polluting its context.

When we use the Repository pattern, we can change the persistence logic for a domain entity once. It applies everywhere the repository is used, with no agent hunting through 40 files, guessing what persistence logic to edit and how.

Add a solid test suite, and the agent gets fast feedback the moment it breaks something the tests actually cover.

Now replace "agent" with "human" in everything I just wrote. Nothing changes!

They are the same practices that let us hold a system in our heads without getting overwhelmed every time a change ripples through ten other files.

A well-designed system is the best way to engineer your context.

posts.content:
"Bro, code is SO cheap now. Quality is dead, just let the agents cook."

AI agents can pump out code faster than we've ever seen, so quality doesn't matter much anymore. Why invest time in quality when the AI agent can blast through the codebase and do the work anyway?

I think the exact opposite is true.

Software quality matters more than ever in the AI age! Not only that, but AI agents are far more sensitive to bad code than humans are.

Let me explain why.

First, what is "quality"? A widely accepted definition is that a good codebase is easy to change. Is the related logic grouped? Will a small change ripple into unintended consequences? Will your feedback loops catch a bug before it hits production?

Add to this that every time someone (or something) touches a codebase, they usually leave it a little messier than they found it. At every change thing get messier and messier, until someone decides to start refactoring and cleaning things up. And this mess compounds at every iteration, creating a terrible place to work for both humans and agents.

Remember, AI agents learn from three things: your prompt, your steering (CLAUDE.md, skills), and your codebase. But it's the codebase that wins every time. It's the source of truth. So even if you explicitly warn against a bad pattern in your steering, the agent will happily copy that pattern straight out of your existing code, no taste applied.

"So no, bro! Code ain't cheap. Mess is cheap. Quality is what keeps your agents cookin' "

posts.content:
Spending a full day in Claude Code leaves my head fried. An endless river of text scrolls past, and buried somewhere in there are the intentions of the LLM that created its own mental model of the problem at hand. Turns out there's a name for why this hurts:
 
It's called Miller's Law.
 
A 1956 paper found that working memory holds about 7 things at once, called "chunks". A chunk can be a single digit, a word, or a whole idea. Keep pouring new ones in, and the old ones fall out the back.
 
Think about booking a flight. You scan option 1, then 4, then 9, comparing price against time. By the time you hit the bottom, you've forgotten what made option 4 good, so you scroll back up. And lose your place again. That's what happens when we ignore Miller's Law in UX design.
 
A terminal agent does the same thing, except the stream never stops. Every tool call, every diff, every log line fights for the same 7 slots. No wonder it's exhausting.
 
UX designers solved this years ago. It's called chunking: group what belongs together so you can grab it in a single glance. On a flight site, you pin your shortlist to a sticky bar that follows you as you scroll down the page. The comparison stops living in your head.
 
So I started asking a simple question: what does chunking look like for an agent in a terminal when I'm planning a new feature?
 
That's what I've been building with a skill called /feature-plan. Instead of planning a feature across 300 lines of scrollback, it collapses the whole thing into one artefact you take in at a glance: the mockup, the story map, an architecture diagram with self-explanatory tooltips, the decisions still open, all in one place.
 
The terminal's stuck in the 80s. Our working memory's stuck in 1956. Might as well design for both.
 
I've started adding my skills to my new repo: https://lnkd.in/dZQKVk46

What have you done to improve your experience with agents?

article.title: GitHub - peppesilletti/skills: Claude Code skills for modern product engineers — from hunch to shipped feature, without losing product sense, design taste, or engineering rigor.
article.subtitle: github.com
article.linkLabel: Open article: GitHub - peppesilletti/skills: Claude Code skills for modern product engineers — from hunch to shipped feature, without losing product sense, design taste, or engineering rigor. by github.com

posts.content:
Why are products designed and built by software engineers typically so bad in terms of UX?

Blame a law most engineers have never heard of.

In the 1980s, Larry Tesler (the Xerox PARC guy who gave us copy and paste) noticed that every application carries a fixed amount of complexity. You can't delete it. You can only decide who deals with it: the person building the product or the person using it.

That's Tesler's Law, the conservation of complexity.

Engineers (and I've been guilty of this too) tend to push complexity away from the code because the code is the part we own and feel. So the user gets a date field that demands YYYY-MM-DD, a settings page with 40 toggles, and an error that says "transaction failed (code 5012)". The product got simpler to build, but more difficult to use for the users.

And it doesn't need to be an actual product. As engineers, we felt this every time a dev in the past decided to make hard-to-change architectural design decisions, making it very difficult for future devs (the code's users) to work with it and think about it.

Good UX is the opposite trade. Detecting the card type from the number, picking a sane default instead of asking, retrying instead of erroring. Each one costs extra engineering hours, and each one is invisible when done right. 

That's the real job: absorbing complexity so your users don't have to.

Next time a design feels "too hard to build", consider that the complexity was always there. Someone was going to pay for it, and it shouldn't be your user.

postedAt.postedAgoText: 6 days ago • Visible to anyone on or off LinkedIn

posts.content:
Most engineers think their work is done when the code reaches production. But production is where the feedback loop starts.
 
For most teams, the pattern is familiar: feature shipped, ticket closed, PR merged, move on. We rarely find out what happened next. Did people use it? Did it solve the problem? Did it make any difference to the business?
 
To close that feedback loop, engineers need to know what change a feature was supposed to create and how to observe it. That’s where understanding the difference between business outcomes and product outcomes becomes useful.
 
Business outcomes are things like revenue, churn, or market share. They matter, but they’re lagging indicators. By the time churn goes up, the bad experience that caused it may have happened weeks ago. You’re looking in the rear-view mirror.
 
Product outcomes measure a behaviour your team can actually influence. “Reduce churn” is a business outcome. “Increase the percentage of users who complete onboarding” is a product outcome.
 
The second gives the team something concrete to design for, measure, and improve. If more users complete onboarding successfully, fewer of them may churn later. That “may” matters, because product development is a bet, not a predictable assembly line. You change a behaviour you believe will affect the business, then measure whether you were right.
 
Engineers already work this way when debugging. We form a hypothesis, inspect the logs, make a small change, and observe what happens. Product development should use the same loop, except we’re observing user behaviour instead of system behaviour.
 
This also changes how we talk about technical work. “We need to refactor authentication” is easy to postpone. “Login takes three seconds and half our users drop at that step” connects the same work to an outcome the whole business understands.
 
An output is the thing you ship. An outcome is what changes because you shipped it.
 
So maybe “done” shouldn’t mean deployed. Maybe it should mean validated.
 
Can you name the product outcome behind the last feature you shipped?

posts.content:
Software engineers are (in)famous for creating UIs that suck. But there is one dead-simple design mental model that can stop us from building absolute trash.

Some time ago, I decided to start studying product design and get better at it. After a couple of courses on Udemy and reading some articles online, I finally opened Figma, only to find out  I had no clue what to do on that blank page. 

I’d learned how to use the tools, but I hadn't built the mindset.

There's one concept that can help us here, and it's really similar to the concept of "let's not reinvent the wheel" that we use as engineers when we decide to use an existing OSS library to solve part of our technical problem.

It's called Jacob's law.

In a nutshell, Jakob's Law states: 
👉 Users spend most of their time on other sites. This means they expect your product to work exactly like the ones they already know.

For engineers, this is the ultimate design hack. It is the visual equivalent of choosing an existing OSS library instead of writing a state management framework from scratch.

Think about modern web apps:
- Clicking your profile picture in the top-right corner is how you open Settings. 
- Finding a shopping cart in the top-right is how you check out on an e-commerce site. 

Picasso once said: "Learn the rules like a pro, so you can break them like an artist." Bending the rules is for geniuses with proven data to back it up. 

For the rest of us normal people, let's just leverage existing UX patterns to build interfaces that don't suck.

What's your trick to make UX suck less as an engineer?

posts.content:
"Significant burnout jumped from 44.7% to 55.7% in one year, while career optimism fell from 54.8% to 48.7%. A worrisome trend." I’m not surprised, and I think this trend started long before AI. Let's take software engineers. 

We engineers have always been at the end of the “assembly line”, taking tickets from Jira, implementing feature after feature, and rarely seeing the impact of our work on users or the business.

As I like to say, we’ve always been the AI agents of the product team.

AI has made this even worse. Feature factories are now producing features 10x faster, asking engineers to push, push, push, and focus their attention on reviewing endless PRs filled with AI-generated slop.

This is not sustainable! And, in my opinion, it doesn’t make much sense, considering that the biggest bottleneck has always been getting feedback from the market and from users.

If AI reduces the time required to write code, that extra capacity shouldn’t automatically be filled with more delivery work. It should give engineers the space to broaden their skills and become more involved in product discovery, design, customer conversations, and strategic decision-making.

Giving engineers ownership of more of the product problem-solving process would also remove many of the inefficiencies created by handoffs, like losing context and delays.

When the people building the solution are closer to the users, the problem, and the desired outcome, teams can learn faster, make better decisions, and avoid translating the same context across multiple roles.

That’s how we can focus on what we do best: solving real problems.

repost.content:
The tech workforce is splitting in two

A year ago, we ran the first large-scale survey of how tech workers feel about their jobs and careers. What emerged we summarized in four words: burned out, but optimistic. Today, we're back with the results from our 2026 survey, and it's a tale of two workforces.

Half of tech right now feels amplified by AI—more capable, more confident, more excited than they've been in their entire career.

The other half feels shaken by it—less sure of their value and whether there’s still a place for them.

Which side of that line you fall on predicts how you feel about your career more than anything else, including your role, seniority, company size, or any other measure we collected. 

The workforce is bifurcating into two realities.

A few other takeaways that surprised us:
+ Significant burnout jumped from 44.7% to 55.7% in one year, while career optimism fell from 54.8% to 48.7%. A worrisome trend.
+ 53% of tech workers would steer a newcomer away from a career in their own role, even when they're optimistic about their own future.
+ The biggest AI fear is of being squeezed to do more work. Only 22% worry about “losing my job to AI.” Far more worry about being expected to do more for the same pay, getting trapped in an unsustainable pace, and the quality of their work declining.

The question that best predicts how a tech worker feels about their work, in 2026, is no longer "What do you do?" or "Where do you work?" It’s "What has AI done to your sense of who you are?"

Read the full report here: https://lnkd.in/gKq4E2uC

(Massive shoutout to my partner Noam Segal for designing the survey, synthesizing the results, and writing this report, two years running. We're dropping a special podcast episode this Sunday, diving even deeper into the results.)

posts.content:
AI gave pair programming its coup de grace. Convincing two engineers to sit at one keyboard and share a brain felt, to most people, like a great way to pay two salaries for one developer. Now those same developers are watching an agent crank out code on its own, and you want to tell them to go "pair up"? Good luck.

For the brave few who actually practised it, pair programming had a dirty little secret: it actually worked. It caught errors in real-time, before they could make a mess. No waiting three days for some passive-aggressive PR review to find out you broke the main branch. You checked quality continuously. 

We need to pack up that exact philosophy and take it with us into the AI era.

In my ten years of building products, I’ve learned that slow coding isn't what kills speed. It's that silos and handoffs create an unbelievable amount of waste, friction, and bureaucratic nonsense. But with AI, we finally have a way to kill them for good.

Here's what I think we could do:

👉 1. Embrace the convergence of roles.
Stop keeping people in neat, tidy little boxes. The boundaries between product, design, and engineering are dissolving, and that’s a good thing. We need to breed a new species of cross-functional builders who can own a problem end-to-end.

👉 2. Kill the handoff.
When you have cross-functional builders, handoffs have no reason to exist. If there’s a vacuum, someone steps in and fills it. No waiting for Jira tickets, no permission slips, no bs.

👉 3. Pair up on the 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘣𝘭𝘦𝘮𝘴, not the code.
Apply the exact same philosophy of pair programming to the entire product development lifecycle. Pair up to run user interviews. Pair up to prioritise. Pair up to sketch.

By pairing teammates on actual product problems, we review quality continuously. No more waiting for bloated weekly meetings. We iterate on the fly, together.

I think this is the future of building things: continuous improvement and relentless quality control, completely stripped of the communication tax, the gatekeeping, and the intellectual silos that have plagued us all along.

AI is finally giving us the freedom to work this way.

posts.content:
I’m excited to share that I’ve hired my first employee!

Ok, not really.

I’ve been experimenting with Hermes lately and created 3 little agents to help me with different activities. So far, the feedback is quite positive. I think they might pass the test period.

What makes Hermes interesting is that it improves based on how you use it. It can create skills, remember preferences from previous interactions, and slowly adapt to the way you work.

For example, I created “The Product Engineer”, an agent that helps me turn ideas into working prototypes when I’m AFK.

I configured it to talk with me on Slack and to use Claude Code interactively through tmux. For now, its brain is GPT-5.5, which I can use through my €18 ChatGPT subscription. Sweet.

After working together for a while, it now knows some of my preferences.

If I ask for a quick POC, I don’t care much about code quality, tests, or perfect architecture. I just want to see if the idea has legs.

But if we’re building something serious, it works differently: BDD, tests written the way I like, vertical slices, then eventually a PR and an ngrok URL so I can review and test the app myself.

Talking with it through Slack feels very different from using Claude Code directly. It’s a bit like talking to an alien who just landed on Earth and needs guidance. Or, more realistically, like onboarding a new teammate. You explain things, correct them, repeat yourself a bit, and slowly they start to understand how you work.

That’s the part I like the most: I can throw an idea at it from anywhere, and it can start turning it into something I can actually test.

The weird part is that it doesn’t feel like using a tool anymore.

It feels like onboarding someone. A very strange someone!

posts.content:
"AI writes the code now. So the real skill for engineers is deciding what to build." I'd love for this to be true, but I'm quite skeptical of statements that completely ignore the context of how people work.

Deciding what to build is a power dynamic, and that's a problem AI won't solve.

Let me tell you a quick story:

A team I worked with wanted to ship a new feature. Their only justification was "we think it's good," and no one spent a single second verifying if it actually brought value to the users.

So I suggested doing the boring thing first: talk to a user (really, one!) to see if it was even worth building. We spent over an hour arguing about this on a call. The PM dismissed the idea of user research entirely without any clear reason, so we built it anyway.

Then the session replays came in. Users toggled the feature on, got immediately confused, and toggled it right back off.

We wasted an hour arguing, a few days implementing, and even more time trying to fix it. Imagine how much we could have learned, and the time we would have saved, if we had just spent 10 minutes talking to a user.

That's why I'm skeptical. As long as companies gatekeep access to users, limit the freedom to experiment, and avoid accountability for outcomes, "deciding what to build" is just an empty slogan.

We talk non-stop about AI context nowadays, "give the right context to the LLM", and I think it's the same for us.
 
We need the right context to produce good outputs. If we only see one part of the whole, or get a diluted version of the truth, the output (or better, outcome) we produce will be less ideal than if we could get better context.
 
There's also a matter of speed and productivity. No man-in-the-middle. Fewer boundaries. More creativity.
 
I'm living this right now with a startup I'm helping during GTM. I get on discovery calls with customers, and something interesting happens in my head, different light bulbs start switching on and off at the right time.

While they're talking, I'm deliberately keeping the solution thinking shut off. I don't want to jump to "we could build X." I'm trying to understand the problem on its own terms, independently from any solution. What's actually breaking for them? Where does it hurt? 

What have they already tried?

But at the same time — and this is the part that's hard to turn off — I'm already thinking about technical constraints. Not to design the thing yet, but because I know the constraints ARE part of the design. They shape what's even worth exploring.

For a long time I thought the answer was finding the right company.

The one that doesn't treat software engineers like code monkeys. Where you get to think about the problem, not just the ticket. Where you can actually have an impact on what gets in users’ hands.

I mean, they exist! But I've realised that finding one is mostly luck: you need to be in right place, right time, right team, right moment in that team's life. You can do everything right and still land somewhere that has no interest in trying a slightly different approach.

(and how arrogant of you to challenge the status-quo!)

The thing is, I don’t like gambling on my professional growth!

Growth needs the freedom to try things, get them wrong, and try again. If that freedom depends on rolling the dice on an employer, or worse, on working with the wrong people, that’s not really in my hands.

So I'd rather build those conditions myself, through the work I take on, and eventually the thing I want to create.

Maybe at some point I'll join a company again, but if I do, I'll be very careful who I lend my time to.

posts.content:
Code reviews are a terrible place for context sharing.

The moment you open a PR, the reviewer should already have the context they need:

- The product goal
- The technical design
- The implementer's intent

Trying to reverse-engineer all of this from a diff is impossible, and it’s unthinkable to be learning about that every single review.

The context needs to be understood way before a single line of code is written: during product discovery, solution design, or team syncs.

The code review should be a “contract review”, meaning, we get there with a clear understanding of what we’re expecting, and we only check that the contract between spec and implementation was respected.
 
And this remains true whether a human or an AI agent is writing the code.

Think about it: would your AI agent be able to learn anything about your context from a PR? I bet not really!

posts.content:
Software engineers are very good at writing tests that explain how the code works. We’re not very good at writing tests that show whether the feature works for a user.
 
I’ve seen plenty of tests that looked something like this:
 
• Mock the repository.
• Call a method.
• Check that another method was called with the right arguments.
 
All lights were green until someone refactored the implementation: the feature behaved the same, and half the tests broke. That's because the tests weren’t protecting behaviour, but its current implementation.
 
There’s a simple mental model that can help us here: think in scenarios.
 
A scenario describes three things:
 
👉 Given a user is in a specific situation 
👉 When they do something 
👉 Then they observe an outcome
 
For example:
 
Given an item is in the cart,
when the user checks out,  
then the order is confirmed.
 
Notice what’s missing: service names, database tables, function calls, and internal state.
  
This way of thinking is useful for two things mainly:
 
-> Before writing code, scenarios force us to design the feature around real user journeys, including the edge cases we usually discover too late.

-> The scenarios can be translated into automated tests that work as documentation, even before a line of code is written. I like to mix E2E browser tests for critical paths and E2E API tests for most scenarios

And of course, you can use AI to build the tests starting from a scenario you've written the old-fashioned way
